instructions.name: cancel_slash
docs: Withdraw a pending judgement on an arbitration outcome. Admin-signed; releases the
reservation; moves no money.

instructions.name: deposit_stake
docs: Add to a provider's bonded stake. Any funder — this is also how the treasury compensates
an overturned judgement.

accounts.name: funder
docs: Whoever funds the deposit. Not required to be the provider: this is also how the
treasury compensates an overturned executed judgement, and a deposit can only ever
increase what the provider owns.

instructions.name: execute_slash
docs: Phase two: the delay was served, the key can still sign, the execution window has not
closed, and the penalty is paid under both caps. Permissionless — the record is the
authority.

instructions.name: expire_slash
docs: Release the reservation of a proposal nobody will act on — the key was revoked or
expired, or the grace period ran out. Permissionless: a hold anybody can end is a hold
nobody can extend.

accounts.name: slash_record
docs: The proposal being reaped. **Declared first**, because the two accounts below are derived
from fields on it and Anchor resolves in declaration order. Its own seeds are
self-referential (`request_id` is stored on it and is what seeded it), which is safe for
the reason `execute_slash` gives: this program is the only writer, and it wrote the
identity and the canonical bump together.

accounts.name: stake
docs: Whose reservation is released. Derived from the record, so the caller cannot free one
provider's hold by naming another's account — there is no attestation here to cross-check
against, so the derivation is the whole of the binding.

accounts.name: verifier_key
docs: The registry entry of the key that proposed, pinned to the record's `verifier` rather than
to the account's own stored key. Half the expiry condition is read from it, so a
substituted entry would let a caller reap a live proposal by presenting some *other* key's
revoked registration.

instructions.name: initialize_config
docs: One-time setup: the admin, the mint, the treasury, every economic parameter and the
pooled stake vault. The signer becomes the admin.

accounts.name: admin
docs: Becomes `Config.admin`. `Config` is a singleton, so this runs exactly once.

accounts.name: config
docs: The stake mint must belong to **SPL Token**, and this is where that is refused. The
constraint hangs off `config` — the first `init` field — because Anchor emits every
`init` block before any non-init constraint, and a Token-2022 mint handed to the SPL
Token program would otherwise fail inside `stake_vault`'s init with an opaque loader
error rather than a refusal this program named.
Why refuse at all: a Token-2022 mint can carry a transfer fee, a transfer hook or a
permanent delegate, each of which breaks `stake_vault.amount >= total_staked`. USDC is
SPL Token, and `Config.stake_mint` is written once, so this is the only moment the
choice can be refused.

accounts.name: stake_vault
docs: The pooled stake vault. Its authority is the config PDA, so stake can only leave
through this program's instructions.

instructions.name: open_escrow
docs: Create one buyer's escrow and the token account that is their balance. Any signer pays
the rent; non-zero limits need the buyer's own signature.

accounts.name: buyer
docs: the limits are non-zero (see the handler); otherwise the buyer proves control by signing
`set_escrow_limits`, `request_withdraw` and `withdraw`, and by the ed25519 signature
every redemption is checked against.

instructions.name: open_stake
docs: Create a provider's stake account.

accounts.name: provider
docs: the provider proves control by signing `request_unstake` and `withdraw_stake`.

instructions.name: propose_slash
docs: Phase one of a slash: prove the verifier's signature, reserve the stake, and start the
72-hour clock. Moves no money.

accounts.name: payer
docs: Pays rent and fees. Being the submitter grants nothing.

accounts.name: instructions_sysvar
docs: `load_instruction_at_checked`, which re-checks the address itself.

instructions.name: redeem_voucher
docs: Pay one provider for one request out of one buyer's escrow, on the buyer's ed25519
signature over the voucher. Permissionless; the fee goes to the treasury's derived ATA
and the rest to the provider's. In the paused set.

accounts.name: rent_payer
docs: The platform's redeemer key, and nobody else — see `Config::redeemer` for why the door
stopped being permissionless. It pays rent and fees and is consulted about nothing else.

accounts.name: escrow
docs: Derived from the **signed** `payer`, so a voucher cannot be aimed at another buyer's
escrow off chain; the `pay_to` check in the handler makes the signed field mean the same.

accounts.name: provider_stake
docs: Derived from the signed `provider`; read for the stake floor only.

accounts.name: treasury_token_account
docs: The treasury's associated token account for the stake mint, derived from
`Config.treasury` — a destination the submitter cannot choose. Created once at
deployment; a redemption against a missing treasury ATA fails until it exists.

accounts.name: instructions_sysvar
docs: `load_instruction_at_checked`, which re-checks the address itself.

instructions.name: register_verifier
docs: Add a verifier signing key to the on-chain allowlist. Admin-only; the key may sign at once.

instructions.name: request_unstake
docs: Start the unbonding clock for `amount`. The amount stays slashable throughout.

instructions.name: request_withdraw
docs: Start a buyer's exit clock, or cancel it with `amount == 0`. Buyer-signed, never paused.

instructions.name: revoke_verifier
docs: Take a verifier signing key out of the allowlist. One-way; the entry is never reusable,
and every pending judgement the key signed becomes reapable.

instructions.name: set_escrow_limits
docs: Change a buyer's own per-call and rolling-window spending ceilings. Buyer-signed.

instructions.name: set_paused
docs: Emergency stop. Admin-only, reversible, and it never closes a door a user leaves by.

instructions.name: update_config
docs: Change the admin or any parameter without upgrading the program. Every field optional;
`None` leaves it alone; every change applies in the slot it arrives. The admin handover
is one step and is applied last; the zero key is refused.

instructions.name: withdraw
docs: Take a matured escrow withdrawal — `min(requested, balance)` — to a token account the
buyer names. Never paused.

accounts.name: config
docs: Read for `stake_mint` only. **Not `mut`, and no pause check** — see the type doc.

accounts.name: destination
docs: Where the money goes. The buyer names it and signs for it; the program does not pin its
owner, because a key that could redirect this is already a key that could withdraw — the
argument `withdraw_stake.rs` makes about its own destination.
It may not be the escrow's own token account: that transfer moves nothing while the
accounting below still debits, which is the shape of a broken balance. Anchor's
duplicate-mutable refusal catches it first in practice; the constraint is here because the
property is ours, not the framework's.

accounts.name: stake_mint
docs: Pinned to `Config`, which is the only end of this that is not the caller's choice. Pinning
it to `escrow_token_account.mint` instead — as this did before — binds nothing at all; see
the type doc.

instructions.name: withdraw_stake
docs: Take matured, unreserved stake out of the program.

accounts.name: destination
docs: Any token account for the mint. Not the vault itself: a vault-to-vault transfer moves
nothing while the accounting below still debits.

types.name: BuyerEscrow
docs: One buyer's escrow — `["escrow", buyer]`.
The token account's authority is a PDA derived from the buyer and nothing else, and exactly
two instructions move tokens out of it — `redeem_voucher`, which needs an ed25519 signature
by `buyer` over an exact amount for an exact request, and `withdraw`, which the buyer signs.
That is the property this program exists for: *even if the env vars holding the private keys
leak, users must not lose money*.
**The balance is not a field here.** It is `escrow_token_account.amount`, the associated
token account of this PDA, which is what makes funding an escrow an ordinary SPL transfer.
# The buyer's signature is a ceiling only if the buyer chose it
The backend writes the HTTP 402, so it picks the amount, the provider and the request, and
the buyer's agent signs what it is asked for. `max_voucher_amount` and `max_per_window` are
what turn the signature into a real bound, because the buyer sets them in advance, on chain,
in a transaction the buyer signs — `set_escrow_limits`, or `open_escrow` co-signed.
# `_reserved` reserves layout
A future field is carved *out of* the array, never appended after it, so every live escrow
stays readable.

fields.name: buyer
docs: The buyer, and the PDA seed. The only key that may `set_escrow_limits`,
`request_withdraw` or `withdraw`, and the key whose ed25519 signature every redemption
is proved against. Written from the `buyer` account, which is also the seed — one source
for this identity, so it cannot disagree with itself.

fields.name: seq_high
docs: The highest sequence number ever redeemed for this buyer. `0` means none, which is
unambiguous only because `seq` is 1-based. **Strictly increasing**: a voucher whose `seq`
is at or below this is dead, whether or not it was ever redeemed. That is the whole
replay rule — see [`admit_seq`](Self::admit_seq).

fields.name: withdraw_requested
docs: What the buyer has asked to take out. `0` when no request stands, which
`request_withdraw(0)` is how a buyer reaches deliberately.

fields.name: withdraw_available_at
docs: When that request matures — `requested_at + WITHDRAW_DELAY_SECONDS`.

fields.name: total_redeemed
docs: Lifetime total redeemed out of this escrow. Monotonic.

fields.name: total_withdrawn
docs: Lifetime total withdrawn by the buyer. Monotonic.

fields.name: max_voucher_amount
docs: The most any single voucher may take from this escrow. **`0` refuses every voucher.** An
escrow whose limits were never armed fails closed; a buyer who genuinely wants no ceiling
writes `u64::MAX`.

fields.name: max_per_window
docs: The most that may be redeemed out of this escrow in a rolling `SLASH_WINDOW_SECONDS`
(24 h). **`0` refuses every voucher**, for the reason above.

fields.name: spent_in_window
docs: What has been redeemed inside that window, drained continuously by [`decay_window`].

fields.name: window_started_at
docs: When `spent_in_window` was last written. `0` until this escrow's first redemption.

fields.name: _reserved
docs: Layout reserved for future fields — carve out of it, never append after it.

types.name: CancelReason
docs: Why a pending judgement stopped being pending without executing.
`Withdrawn` is the admin's decision on an arbitration outcome. `Expired` is the platform
failing to execute its own judgement inside the grace period. `VerifierUnavailable` is a
revocation reaching through and killing work in flight, which is the property the whole
two-phase design exists to deliver.

types.name: Config
docs: Program configuration, economic parameters and custody totals — `["config"]`, the only
singleton.
Every number the program enforces is a field here rather than a constant in the code: a
renegotiated term must not be a program upgrade. The program keeps only *bounds*
on these values — see `constants.rs` — and the two delays that guard incident response
(`SLASH_DELAY_SECONDS`, `WITHDRAW_DELAY_SECONDS`) are constants precisely because a delay the
admin key could shorten is a delay a stolen admin key sets to zero.
The layout is free to change until the program is deployed under its final id: this account
is created by `initialize_config` at whatever size the tree builds, and nothing closes it.
`_reserved` is room for a later field without a redeploy — carve a field *out of* the array,
never append after it.

fields.name: admin
docs: May change parameters, pause, enrol and revoke verifier keys, and cancel a pending
judgement. **It can reach provider stake, slowly**: it may enrol a verifier key of its own
and sign a judgement with it, which `execute_slash` pays after `SLASH_DELAY_SECONDS`.
That is the residual `lib.rs` names; the role is a hardware wallet held by a person.

fields.name: stake_mint
docs: The mint every stake deposit, escrow balance and withdrawal is denominated in (USDC on
mainnet). SPL Token only — `initialize_config` refuses Token-2022.

fields.name: treasury
docs: The platform's wallet. **Its associated token account is derived, never passed in** —
see `execute_slash` and `redeem_voucher`. A destination the submitter chooses is a
destination the submitter can point at itself.

fields.name: unbonding_period_seconds
docs: How long stake stays slashable after an unstake request. Bounded by
`MIN_UNBONDING_PERIOD_SECONDS..=MAX_UNBONDING_PERIOD_SECONDS`.
Read live by `ProviderStake::unbonding_matured`, so changing it re-dates every
unbonding already in flight rather than applying only to new ones — see the note at
the write site in `instructions/update_config.rs`.

fields.name: take_rate_bps
docs: The platform's cut of a paid call, taken by `redeem_voucher`. At most `MAX_TAKE_RATE_BPS`.

fields.name: slash_agent_bps
docs: The harmed agent's compensating share of a penalty. **Must be non-zero**: a penalty split
that compensates nobody is a transfer to the platform, and it deletes the half of the
promise that says an agent harmed by a bad provider is compensated.

fields.name: slash_platform_bps
docs: The platform's share of a penalty. `10_000 - agent - platform` stays with the provider.

fields.name: slash_cap_bps
docs: The most of a provider's stake that may be judged against them at any one instant, as a
fraction of `at_risk`. At most `MAX_SLASH_CAP_BPS`.
The counter drains continuously over `SLASH_WINDOW_SECONDS`, so at any *instant* at most
this fraction may be judged and across an *arbitrary* 24-hour interval at most twice it —
see [`decay_window`]. The ceiling is frozen onto each `SlashRecord` at proposal
(`cap_allowance`), so records proposed at the same time against the same stake share one
allowance per window, but a fresh window opens a fresh allowance measured on the stake
held *at proposal*, not on what is left. The bound a leaked verifier key faces is
therefore `cap` of the original stake per day per provider, `verifier_daily_cap` per key,
and `revoke_verifier` as the only hard stop.

fields.name: minimum_stake
docs: The stake floor a provider must hold to be paid. **Enforced on the paying path, never on
the exit**: `redeem_voucher` refuses a provider whose `bonded` is below it
(`ProviderBelowMinimumStake`), because being paid is the counterpart of being slashable,
and `withdraw_stake` never reads it, because a floor on the exit door would convert a
routing rule into capital confiscation. Must be greater than zero — at zero any keypair
is a payable provider with nothing to slash.

fields.name: penalty_amount
docs: The most one judgement may take — a **ceiling** on `attestation.penalty`, enforced by
`propose_slash`. `0` means no provider can be slashed at all, which is the on-chain form
of shadow mode. Deliberately unbounded above: a token amount has no scale-free absurd
value, and what bounds the damage is `slash_cap_bps`, a fraction of the provider's own
stake. Note that a leaked verifier key can *reserve* up to this much per record, so the
number also sizes how cheaply such a key can freeze a provider's exit for the ten days
until the record expires or the key is revoked.

fields.name: verifier_daily_cap
docs: The most one registered verifier key may have judged in a rolling `SLASH_WINDOW_SECONDS`,
across **every** provider, in the mint's base units. `slash_cap_bps` bounds the loss to
one provider; this bounds the reach of one key. Must be greater than zero — a zero cap
would refuse every slash, which is `revoke_verifier`'s job done silently.

fields.name: paused
docs: Emergency stop. Closes `propose_slash`, `execute_slash` and `redeem_voucher` — the doors
that move money on somebody else's say-so — and never a door that returns money to its
owner. See `instructions/set_paused.rs`.

fields.name: total_staked
docs: Σ of every `bonded + unbonding` across all provider stake accounts.

fields.name: total_slashed
docs: Σ of every executed slash, across all providers. There is no on-chain reversal; an
overturned judgement is compensated by a `deposit_stake` from the treasury, which counts
as a deposit.

fields.name: redeemer
docs: The only key that may submit `redeem_voucher`. Redemption used to be permissionless —
the buyer's signature is the whole authority over the money — but `seq` only has to
*increase*, so anyone able to land a redemption could land a dust voucher with a higher
`seq` and void every served-but-unredeemed voucher below it, at the platform's cost.
Pinning the submitter to the platform's own redeemer key closes that for a buyer, a
provider and a stranger alike; a leaked redeemer key can only do what the backend could
already do with the vouchers it holds.
Carved out of `_reserved` (64 → 32 bytes) on 2026-09-04, so it sits here, after the
bumps, rather than beside `treasury`.

fields.name: _reserved
docs: Layout reserved for future fields. **A new field is carved out of this array** (shrink it
and add the field in the freed bytes), never appended after it, so `INIT_SPACE` and every
live account stay readable.

types.name: ConfigInitialized
docs: Every state change emits an event. The off-chain reconciler repairs the ledger from chain
state, and the provider dashboard reads stake and parameters —
both need a stream, not a poll of the current value.
Both config events carry the whole parameter set, changed or not: a watcher whose job is to
notice that a number just moved should not have to hold the previous value to read this one.

fields.name: slash_provider_bps
docs: Derived, not stored — emitted so a reader does not have to know that the provider's
share of a penalty is the remainder of the other two.

types.name: ConfigUpdated
docs: Every parameter change is an on-chain event, so a parameter history can be shown from the
event stream alone.

types.name: EscrowOpened
docs: One buyer's escrow was created, with the two limits it was born under.

fields.name: amount
docs: `min(requested, balance)` — what actually moved.

types.name: PauseToggled
docs: The emergency stop moving in either direction. Carried as a *state* rather than as two
events, because a watcher that joined mid-incident needs to know which way the switch is
sitting, not which transition it just missed.

types.name: ProviderStake
docs: One provider's stake. PDA: `["stake", provider]`.

fields.name: provider
docs: The provider identity. The only key that can unstake or withdraw.

fields.name: bonded
docs: Active stake — backs paid traffic, fully slashable.

fields.name: unbonding
docs: Stake the provider asked to take out. Still fully slashable for the whole unbonding
period; that is the point of the period.

fields.name: unbonding_started_at
docs: When the current unbonding period started. `0` when nothing is unbonding.

fields.name: slashed_in_window
docs: How much has been *judged* against this provider inside the current window, decayed
continuously — see [`decay_window`]. Read lazily, never swept.

fields.name: slash_window_started_at
docs: When this counter was last written, and therefore the point the drain measures from.
`0` until the provider's first slash.

fields.name: pending_slash
docs: Stake reserved by `SlashRecord`s that are still `Pending`, and therefore not
withdrawable — see `withdrawable`. Invariant: `Σ pending_slash == Σ reserved over every
Pending record`, maintained by exactly four writers: `propose_slash` adds;
`execute_slash`, `cancel_slash` and `expire_slash` subtract.

types.name: ResponseClass
docs: How a verified call came out, in the vocabulary the off-chain classifier uses.
The program does not classify anything — that is business logic and belongs off-chain.
It carries the class because the class is *signed*: the response-class table makes
`DATA_FAIL` the only class that may ever touch stake, and putting the field in the message
makes that a chain-enforced rule instead of a backend convention. A `SYSTEM_ERROR`
attestation cannot be re-submitted as a slash, because changing the byte breaks the
signature.
Discriminants are written out and serialised explicitly by `signed_message`, so reordering
this enum cannot silently change what a signature means.

types.name: SlashAttestation
docs: One verifier's signed judgement about one request.
The judgement carries `requestId`, `provider`, `status`, `penalty`, `policy` and
`timestamp`, plus the `expiry` the program checks — and **`beneficiary` as well**.
It has to. The split sends a share of every penalty (60% by default) to the agent that was
harmed, but a slash interface of the form `slash(requestId, provider, penalty, attestation)`
never names that agent. Only two ways to close the gap. Either the program looks the agent
up from the `requestId`, which means the program holds off-chain request state and stops
being pure economic consequence; or the address rides along with the judgement. It rides
along. And once it rides along it must be *inside* the signature, because a beneficiary the
platform can choose after the verifier signed is a beneficiary the platform can set to
itself — the compromised-platform case this file exists to close, arriving through the one
field that is easiest to forget to cover.

fields.name: request_id
docs: The request this judgement is about, and the replay key: one `SlashRecord` PDA per
`request_id`, ever. 32 raw bytes rather than a string — the off-chain id is hashed
into this width, so the seed length is fixed and no id is unrepresentable.
For a window-level penalty this carries the *window* id. The program does not
care which it is; it cares only that the issuer never reuses one.

fields.name: provider
docs: Whose stake is reduced. Seeds the `ProviderStake` PDA, so the account the instruction
touches is derived from the signed bytes rather than chosen by the caller.

fields.name: beneficiary
docs: The harmed agent, who receives the compensating share of the penalty. Recorded on the
slash record and paid by `execute_slash`.

fields.name: status
docs: Must be `DataFail` for a slash. See [`ResponseClass`].

fields.name: penalty
docs: The penalty the verifier judged, in stake-mint base units. What is actually taken may
be less if the provider does not have that much left — both numbers are recorded.

fields.name: policy
docs: Which policy version produced the judgement. The program never interprets
it; it is signed so that a dispute can prove which rules were in force, and so the
platform cannot re-label a verdict after the fact.

fields.name: issued_at
docs: When the verifier signed.

fields.name: expires_at
docs: After this, the program refuses the attestation. Distinct from the *registration*
expiry on `VerifierKey`: a key can be fine while a judgement is stale, and vice versa.

types.name: SlashCancelled
docs: A pending judgement released without executing. See [`CancelReason`].

fields.name: released
docs: The reservation handed back, which is the record's `reserved` and never a partial
amount: a reservation is discharged whole or not at all.

fields.name: pending_slash
docs: The provider's remaining reservation.

types.name: SlashExecuted
docs: Phase two: the delay was served, the key could still sign, and the penalty was paid.

fields.name: released
docs: The reservation handed back — the record's whole `reserved`, of which `applied` was
paid and the rest returned to the provider's free balance.

types.name: SlashProposed
docs: Phase one: a verifier's judgement is on chain, the stake behind it is reserved, and nothing
has moved.
**This is the event the incident response watches.** Between it and `SlashExecuted` there is
`SLASH_DELAY_SECONDS` of wall-clock time in which `revoke_verifier` — a Ledger transaction —
voids this proposal and every other one that key signed.

fields.name: reserved
docs: What was actually set aside — `min(penalty, cap_allowance, free)`.

fields.name: pending_slash
docs: The provider's whole reservation after this one.

types.name: SlashRecord
docs: One judgement. PDA: `["slash", request_id]`.
**Its address is the replay lock**: `init` on `["slash", request_id]` succeeds exactly once,
so an attestation cannot be proposed twice by anybody, including whoever captured the
transaction. It is also the evidence a dispute reads — what was judged, under which policy,
by which key, and what was actually taken. Nothing closes it.

fields.name: beneficiary
docs: The harmed agent, paid `agent_amount` into their **derived** associated token
account by `execute_slash`.

fields.name: verifier
docs: The registered key whose signature authorised this.

fields.name: penalty
docs: What the attestation asked for.

fields.name: applied
docs: What the provider's stake and the caps could actually cover at execution.
`penalty - applied` is the shortfall, recorded rather than retried: the request id is
spent either way.

fields.name: agent_amount
docs: The compensating share that reached the agent.

fields.name: platform_amount
docs: The platform's share, paid to the treasury's derived ATA.

fields.name: slash_agent_bps
docs: The split in force when the judgement executed, so a dispute can name it after the
parameters have moved.

fields.name: attested_at
docs: The attestation's `issued_at` — when the judgement was made, not when it landed.

fields.name: executed_at
docs: When the chain executed it. `0` unless `status == Executed`.

fields.name: status
docs: The `init` on `["slash", request_id]` is the replay lock; this is what stops the second
phase running twice, and it is checked before anything else in `execute_slash`,
`cancel_slash` and `expire_slash`.

fields.name: proposed_at
docs: When `propose_slash` wrote this record.

fields.name: executable_at
docs: `proposed_at + SLASH_DELAY_SECONDS`. Frozen here so that nothing during the wait can pull
a judgement forward. `execute_slash` accepts it from this instant until
`executable_at + SLASH_EXECUTION_GRACE_SECONDS`; from that instant `expire_slash` may
reap it instead.

fields.name: reserved
docs: The stake `propose_slash` set aside — `min(penalty, cap_allowance, at_risk -
pending_slash)`. Added to `ProviderStake::pending_slash` on the way in and subtracted on
the way out, whichever way out it is. **It is also the ceiling on what this judgement may
ever be paid**, so `Σ pending_slash` is an honest upper bound on what every standing
judgement can still reach.

fields.name: cap_allowance
docs: `slash_cap_bps` of the provider's `at_risk` **at proposal time** — the provider's whole
daily ceiling, frozen. Execution pays at most `reserved`, and at most `cap_allowance`
less whatever the provider's rolling window has since carried. Frozen for the same reason
`executable_at` is: a figure re-derived at execution is a figure the party being judged
can move in between.

fields.name: cancelled_at
docs: `0` unless `status == Cancelled`.

types.name: SlashStatus
docs: Where a `SlashRecord` is in its life.
A record leaves `Pending` exactly once, and neither `Executed` nor `Cancelled` has an edge
back out. That is what keeps the reservation accounting (`ProviderStake::pending_slash`)
single-entry — the amount is added on the way in and released on exactly one way out.

fields.name: funder
docs: Whoever paid. The provider themselves in the ordinary case; the treasury when it is
compensating an overturned judgement.

types.name: VerifierKey
docs: One approved verifier signing key. PDA: `["verifier", verifier]`.
This account **is** the allowlist. Expressed as a PDA, "is this key registered" is a seeds
constraint — the runtime refuses to hand the instruction an account at any other address.
Both slash phases take this account and call `assert_can_sign` — phase two so that a
revocation during the wait reaches backwards into a judgement already in flight.

fields.name: verifier
docs: The ed25519 public key that signs attestations, and the PDA seed. Stored as well as
seeded so `assert_can_sign` compares against stored state rather than trusting the
caller's account choice alone.

fields.name: label
docs: Operator-chosen label — `verifier-2026-08`, the key id the off-chain journal records.

fields.name: expires_at
docs: When this key stops being accepted regardless of status. Always in the future at
registration and never further out than `MAX_VERIFIER_KEY_LIFETIME_SECONDS`.

fields.name: revoked_at
docs: `0` while active. Set once, by `revoke_verifier`, and never cleared.

fields.name: slashed_in_window
docs: How much this key has had *judged* inside the current window, decayed continuously —
see [`decay_window`].

fields.name: slash_window_started_at
docs: When this key's counter was last written. `0` until its first executed slash.

types.name: VerifierStatus
docs: Whether a registered verifier key may still sign an attestation the program will accept.
Two states and no third. "Suspended" was considered and rejected: a key that is suspected is
revoked, and a key that is fine is active.

types.name: Voucher
docs: One buyer's signed instruction to pay one provider for one request.
# This is the only thing that can take a buyer's money on somebody else's submission
`redeem_voucher` is permissionless: its signer pays rent and fees and is consulted about
nothing. The authority is entirely in these bytes, proved through the ed25519 precompile
against **`payer`** — which is also the seed of the escrow the money comes out of, so the
account touched is derived from signed data rather than chosen by the submitter.
## The naming convention `redeem_voucher` has to break, and why
**This program already calls the transaction's fee payer `payer`.** Five account structs
declare `pub payer: Signer<'info>`: `open_stake.rs:11`, `cancel_slash.rs:68`,
`execute_slash.rs` and `propose_slash.rs`. That is the
established convention, and copying the neighbouring instruction is the normal and usually
correct instinct — so an implementer writing `RedeemVoucher` will reach for the same name.
**`redeem_voucher` is the one instruction where that is a catastrophe**, because it is the one
instruction that already has a `payer` meaning something else. `voucher.payer` is the *buyer*;
`ctx.accounts.payer` would be the *platform*. With both under one identifier in one function,
```ignore
require_signed_by(&sysvar, &ctx.accounts.payer.key(), &voucher.signed_message())?;
compiles, reads correctly to a reviewer skimming for "the payer signed it", and lets anybody
who can submit a transaction drain every escrow — the key proved is then the submitter's own,
and the submitter chooses it.
So `RedeemVoucher`'s fee account **must** be named `rent_payer`, deliberately departing from
those five. They are not wrong; they simply have no second `payer` to be confused with, and
this instruction does. **The key passed to `require_signed_by` for a voucher is
`voucher.payer` — a field of these signed bytes — and never an account of the instruction.**
# `issued_at` has to be in here, and it is the field the layout was corrected for
An earlier 231-byte draft of this layout carried only `expires_at`, with the five-minute lifetime
enforced by the backend on receipt. The backend is the component the threat model assumes is
compromised, and it authors the HTTP 402 the buyer's agent signs. So without `issued_at` the
program cannot see a voucher's width at all: a 402 quoting `expires_at = now + 90 days` yields
a standing charge against that escrow for three months, and the withdrawal-delay
const-assert —
`WITHDRAW_DELAY > REDEEM_GRACE + VOUCHER_MAX_LIFETIME` — relates two on-chain constants to
one the attacker supplies. With it, [`require_valid_voucher_window`] bounds the whole
redeemable life at `MAX_VOUCHER_REDEEMABLE_LIFE_SECONDS`, on the chain's clock.
# What is deliberately *not* in here
**No destination for the money.** The provider is paid into the associated token account
the program derives from `provider`, and the fee into the one it derives from
`Config::treasury`. A destination in the signed bytes would be one the *buyer* chose; one in
the *accounts* would be one the submitter chose, which is the hole `execute_slash` closes by
deriving the beneficiary's ATA. Deriving both gives neither party the choice.
**No fee.** The split is `Config::take_rate_bps` at redemption time, published in the
`VoucherRedeemed` event. Signing a fee would mean every parameter change invalidated every
voucher in flight, which is the argument `Config::penalty_amount` makes about attestations.

fields.name: payer
docs: **The buyer.** The key whose ed25519 signature is proved, and the seed of the escrow the
money leaves — so it is read out of these signed bytes and is *never* an account the
submitter chose. `redeem_voucher`'s fee account is called `rent_payer` precisely so that
this field has no namesake inside that function; note that five *other* account structs in
this program do name their fee payer `payer`, so the convention being broken there is
deliberate. See the type doc.

fields.name: pay_to
docs: Where the x402 `exact` scheme sent the money — the buyer's escrow PDA. Checked against the
escrow account's own address, which is itself derived from `payer`, so this field is
defence in depth rather than the binding: it is what makes the *off-chain* `payTo` a
signed fact, so a 402 cannot aim a buyer's payment at somebody else's escrow.

fields.name: provider
docs: Who gets paid. Seeds the provider's stake account and derives the associated token
account the payment lands in, so both are derived from the signed bytes.

fields.name: amount
docs: The **exact** price, in the stake mint's base units — not a ceiling. The client learned it
from the 402 and signed that number; the program moves exactly it.

fields.name: resource_hash
docs: `sha256(resource)` — which endpoint was bought. The program never interprets it; it is
signed so a dispute can prove what was paid for.

fields.name: request_hash
docs: The request this voucher pays for. The off-chain replay key; the on-chain one is `seq`.

fields.name: seq
docs: This buyer's monotonic payment counter, issued by `GET /escrow/next-seq` and **1-based**.
The on-chain replay key — see [`BuyerEscrow`](crate::state::BuyerEscrow).

fields.name: issued_at
docs: When the client signed, on the client's clock. Bounds the window's *width*; see the type
doc for why the program cannot do without it. **Declared before `expires_at`, because that
is the order it is signed in** — see [`Voucher::signed_message`].

fields.name: expires_at
docs: After this, plus `REDEEM_GRACE_SECONDS`, the program refuses.

types.name: VoucherRedeemed
docs: One voucher paid: `amount` left the buyer's escrow, `amount - fee` reached the provider's
associated token account and `fee` the treasury's.

fields.name: spent_in_window
docs: The buyer's rolling counter after this redemption, so a reader can watch the cap
approach.

fields.name: amount
docs: `0` means the standing request was cancelled.

constants.name: CONFIG_SEED
docs: Singleton config PDA — `["config"]`.

constants.name: ESCROW_SEED
docs: Per-buyer escrow PDA — `["escrow", buyer]`.
**This account is what makes a leaked platform key worthless.** If a buyer's balance sat in
one pooled vault whose authority the settlement service could sign for, "only the owner
withdraws" would be a property of the service's code rather than of the chain. Here the
authority is a PDA derived from the buyer and nothing else, and exactly two
instructions move tokens out of it: `redeem_voucher`, which needs an ed25519 signature by
the buyer over an exact amount for an exact request, and `withdraw`, which the buyer signs.
There is no admin path beside them.
One account per buyer rather than a map, for the reason [`VERIFIER_SEED`] and [`TERMS_SEED`]
give: a map's length is fixed at `InitSpace` time, so the ten-thousandth buyer would be a
program upgrade, and every payment would rewrite the account every other payment reads.
**Nothing closes an escrow**, so the address is never reused with a reset `seq_high`; the
rent is the price of that.

constants.name: SLASH_DELAY_SECONDS
docs: How long a proposed slash waits before `execute_slash` may pay. A
constant rather than a `Config` field: the delay is the window in which a human holding the
admin key can see `SlashProposed` and revoke the key that signed it, and a delay the admin
key could shorten is a delay a stolen admin key sets to zero.

constants.name: SLASH_RECORD_SEED
docs: Per-slash record PDA — `["slash", request_id]`.
**This seed is the replay defence.** `init` on a PDA whose address is derived from the
signed `request_id` can succeed exactly once, so a captured attestation cannot be
resubmitted — not by a compromised platform, not by anyone who saw the transaction.
Nothing closes these accounts, for the same reason `revoke_verifier` closes nothing: a
reclaimable record is a reusable request id.

constants.name: STAKE_SEED
docs: Per-provider stake PDA — `["stake", provider]`.

constants.name: STAKE_VAULT_SEED
docs: The pooled stake vault token account — `["stake_vault"]`.
One token account for every provider's stake, exactly as the vault holds every agent's
balance in one account. Per-provider ownership lives in the `ProviderStake` PDAs; the
vault only has to satisfy `vault.amount == config.total_staked`.

constants.name: VERIFIER_SEED
docs: Per-verifier registry PDA — `["verifier", verifier_pubkey]`.
**One account per verifier, deliberately — not an array in `Config`.**
The allowlist has to be editable on-chain without a program upgrade, and it has
to grow into a multi-verifier quorum later without a rewrite. A `Vec<Pubkey>` in `Config`
fails both: its length is fixed at `InitSpace` time, so raising the cap *is* an upgrade,
and every registration rewrites the one account every other instruction reads. A PDA per
key makes registration and revocation independent writes, makes the allowlist check a
seeds constraint rather than a linear scan, and makes quorum a matter of passing `n`
accounts instead of a different data structure.

constants.name: WITHDRAW_DELAY_SECONDS
docs: How long a buyer's escrow withdrawal waits between `request_withdraw` and `withdraw`. A
constant for the reason [`SLASH_DELAY_SECONDS`] is, and sized by the assertion below: it
must outlive the longest voucher the program will still redeem, so a call served on a
voucher signed before the request can still be collected.
